'''''Yucca aloifolia'''''<ref name="l">[https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/13829#page/331/mode/1up Linnaeus, Species Plantarum 1: 319. 1753].</ref> is the [[type species]] for the genus ''[[Yucca]]''. Common names include '''aloe yucca''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=YUAL|taxon=Yucca aloifolia|access-date=8 August 2015}}</ref> '''dagger plant''',<ref name="fna"/> and  '''Spanish bayonet'''. It grows in sandy soils, especially on sand dunes along the coast.

==Range==
''Yucca aloifolia'' is native to the [[East Coast of the United States|Atlantic]] and [[Gulf Coast of the United States|Gulf Coasts]] of the United States from southern [[Virginia]] south to [[Florida]] and west to the [[Texas]] Gulf Coast, to Mexico along the [[Yucatán Peninsula|Yucatán]] coast, and to [[Bermuda]], and parts of the [[Caribbean]]. Normally, ''Yucca aloifolia'' is grown in USDA zones 8 through 11. It is a popular landscape plant in beach areas along the lower [[East Coast of the United States|East Coast]] from [[Virginia]] to [[Florida]].

''Yucca aloifolia'' has become naturalized in [[Bahamas]], [[Argentina]], [[Uruguay]], [[Italy]], [[Pakistan]], [[South Africa]], [[Queensland]], [[New South Wales]], and [[Mauritania]]. It is common in gardens and parks of the [[Iberian Peninsula]].<ref>{{cite book |last=López |first=Ginés |date=2007 |title=Guía de los árboles y arbustos de la Península Ibérica y Baleares, 3rd edition | language = es }}</ref>

==Description==
''Yucca aloifolia'' has an erect trunk, {{convert|3|-|5|in|cm|abbr=on}} in diameter, reaching up to {{convert|5|–|20|ft|m|abbr=on}} tall before it becomes top heavy and topples over. When this occurs, the tip turns upward and keeps on growing. The trunk is armed with sharp pointed straplike leaves with fine-toothed edges, each about {{convert|2|ft|m|abbr=on}} long. The young leaves near the growing tip stand erect; older ones are reflexed downward, and the oldest wither and turn brown, hanging around the lower trunk like a Hawaiian skirt. Eventually the tip of the trunk develops a {{convert|2|ft|m|abbr=on}} long spike of white, purplish-tinged flowers, each blossom about 4 in (12.7 cm) across. After flowering, the trunk stops growing, but one or more lateral buds are soon formed, and the uppermost becomes a new terminal shoot. ''Yucca aloifolia'' also produces new buds, or offshoots, near the base of the trunk, forming the typical thicket often observed in dry sandy and scrub beach areas of the southeastern United States.<ref name="fna">[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=220014440 ''Flora of North America'' vol. 26, p. 429. 2006].</ref><ref>CONABIO. 2009. Catálogo taxonómico de especies de México. 1. In Capital Nat. México. CONABIO, Mexico City.</ref><ref>ORSTOM. 1988. List of Vascular Plants of Gabon with Synonymy, Herbier National du Gabon, Yaounde</ref><ref>[http://www.parks.org/pjbot/PDFs/44%28SI1%29/19.pdf Nanwal, H, M Hameed, T Nawaz, MSA Ahmad, A Younis. 2012. Structural adaptations for adaptability in some exotic and naturalized species of Agavaceae. Pakistani Journal of Botany 44 (special issue):129.134.]</ref><ref>[http://apps.kew.org/wcsp/namedetail.do?name_id=291591 Kew World Checklist of Selected Plant Families, ''Yucca aloifolia'']</ref><ref>[http://luirig.altervista.org/flora/taxa/index1.php?scientific-name=yucca+aloifolia Altervista Flora Italiana, Jucca]</ref>

''Yucca aloifolia'' flowers are white and showy, sometimes tinged purplish, so that the plant is popular as an ornamental. Fruits are elongated, fleshy, up to 5 cm long. It is widely planted in hot climates and arid environments.<ref name="fna" /><ref>Davidse, G., M. Sousa Sánchez & A.O. Chater. 1994. Alismataceae a Cyperaceae. 6: i–xvi, 1–543. In G. Davidse, M. Sousa Sánchez & A.O. Chater (eds.) Flora Mesoamericana. Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, México, D. F.</ref><ref>Whalen, E.E. 1902. Killarney Gardening Newsletter 14(May):19-23</ref><ref>Wunderlin, R. P. 1998. Guide to the Vascular Plants of Florida i–x, 1–806. University Press of Florida, Gainesville.</ref><ref>Radford, A. E., H. E. Ahles & C. R. Bell. 1968. Manual of the Vascular Flora of the Carolinas i–lxi, 1–1183. University of North Carolina Press, Chapel Hill.</ref><ref>Long, R. W. & O. K. Lakela. 1971. Flora of Tropical Florida: A Manual of the Seed Plants and Ferns of Southern Peninsular Florida i–xvii, 1–962. University of Miami Press, Coral Cables</ref>

The tree has a short lifespan and can live up to 50 years[https://www.flawildflowers.org/flower-friday-yucca-aloifolia/].

==Uses==
The fruit is eaten by both birds and humans, and the flowers can be eaten cooked or raw.<ref>{{cite book|last=Little|first=Elbert L.|title=The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Trees: Eastern Region|publisher=Knopf|location=New York|year=1980|isbn=0-394-50760-6|page=317}}</ref>

''Yucca aloifolia''{{'}}s roots can be used as soap and shampoo.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.practicalsurvivor.com/usefulplants|title=Useful Plants | Practical Survivor}}</ref>
